newsitem.title: GERMANY: German jobs turnaround still nowhere in sight.
newsitem.headline: German jobs turnaround still nowhere in sight.

text.p: Germany's long-awaited turnaround on the jobs market was still nowhere to be seen on Thursday amid reports of disappointing May numbers and an admission by Finance Minister Theo Waigel that the economy was not helping.

The official figures, due on Friday, come as Germany courts increasing unpopularity with continued opposition to a European Union employment chapter, a stance that could lead to political risks for Chancellor Helmut Kohl at home.

Two German newspapers reported that unemployment in May, not adjusted for seasonal variations, fell just 90,000, much less than normal for a period in which strong economic activity traditionally boosts the jobs market.
The Berliner Zeitung said unadjusted unemployment declined by around 90,000 to 4.25 million people.
But the paper said if economic revival in May had been as strong as it has been in past years during the same month, unemployment should have dropped by 150,000.

The mass circulation Bild newspaper said the jobless total fell by 91,000 in May to 4.255 million, before seasonal adjustment, citing data from the Federal Labour Office, the body that gathers and publishes the figures.
The Office was not immediately available to confirm the figures, which also fall below the expectations of many German economists.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, asked by reporters to comment on new data showing German economic growth at just 0.5 percent quarter-on-quarter, was downbeat in his assessment of the overall picture.
"The latest indicators are more positive but unfortunately they are not yet impacting the labour market," he told journalists in Hamburg, where he was giving a speech.
If that is the case, Bonn's resistance to Europe-wide job-creation measures due to be discussed at the Amsterdam EU summit on June 16 could yet be politically untenable.

Speaking on the main evening news programme of Germany's ARD public television station, EU Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies said recent left-wing poll victories in London and Paris were making Germany, which argues employment policy is best handled nationally, appear more and more isolated.

"We've got the wind in our sails now. Not only will we get an employment chapter in Amsterdam worth the name but leaders will also pass through some 80 employment pacts that we want to finance with the structural fund," said Wulf-Mathies, who is a member of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

Wulf-Mathies added she was "fairly certain" Bonn would lift its opposition to such measures and that it would see they did not contradict the tenets of the social market economy, the system that has served Germany since World War Two.

Germany's refusal to budge on the issue during a meeting of foreign ministers in Luxembourg this week gave the opposition SPD welcome material with which to attack the government on what is the top domestic political issue.

Trade unions, too, are annoyed by Bonn's stance, with the German Trade Union Federation on Wednesday denouncing Foreign Ministry State Secretary Werner Hoyer's position in Luxembourg as a cyncial blocking tactic ahead of Amsterdam.
